surface_forms: un aventurier du nom de Swann

appraisal_events.evidence: "un homme considérable qui venait, dans un procès fameux, de donner un témoignage dont la seule valeur résidait dans sa haute moralité devant laquelle les juges et les avocats s'étaient unanimement inclinés"; "il y eut un mouvement de curiosité et de déférence quand il entra. C'était Morel. J'étais peut-être seul à savoir qu'il avait été entretenu par M. de Charlus, puis par Saint-Loup".
appraisal_events.explanation: The assembled company receives Morel with curiosity and deference as a public paragon of moral authority, and the delayed naming ("C'était Morel") plus the narrator's private knowledge that he was a kept man turns that collective elevation into open irony rather than endorsement.

appraisal_events.evidence: "ouvrages sans originalité, mais qui donnaient aux jeunes gens et à beaucoup de femmes du monde l'impression d'une hauteur intellectuelle peu commune, d'une sorte de génie"; "il avait fait, pour une phase nouvelle de sa vie, honorée, glorieuse, une apparition de grand homme"; "on ne pensait pas qu'il eût jamais vécu ailleurs".
appraisal_events.explanation: In the reconstituted salon Bloch is received as a great man of established standing, the amnesia of the new society erasing his earlier "piètre figure"; the narrator undercuts the acclaim by calling his books unoriginal and their reasoning an "absurde sophistique".

status_effects.explanation: Morel's local standing rises sharply: judges, lawyers and now the salon bow before his supposed moral authority, and his entrance produces a movement of deference.
The narrator's disclosure that this paragon of "haute moralité" was kept successively by Charlus and Saint-Loup deflates him in the reader's estimation even as society honors him.
Bloch passes from the man who cut a poor figure in his old milieux to a glorious, honored presence taken for a lifelong fixture of the great world.
The narrator qualifies the acclaim by judging his books unoriginal and their sophistry absurd, and by noting his prestige is backdated on a few names picked up through Saint-Loup.

ambiguities: "La princesse de Guermantes" occurs twice with plausibly different referents: in the retrospective sentence about the old dinners it points to Marie-Gilbert, whereas the present hostess whose salon the newcomers invade, and who the young believe "avait toujours eu la plus grande situation", fits the remarried Mme Verdurin now bearing the title. The passage does not disambiguate.
